deltas.old: You hang your hat on the third peg, brim out. Across the room a man sets his cup down and lets you see him look at you.
deltas.new: Your hat goes onto the third peg, brim out, ninth of nine. A man by the window lowers his cup an inch and holds it there, watching you do it.

deltas.old: The coat is already over the chair back. You lay yours beside it, lift the wrong one on the way past, and the hearth chairs stay exactly as full as they were.
deltas.new: Your coat goes over the chair back with the package folded into it, alongside the coat already hanging there. Two steps later you have the other coat over your arm and the door in front of you.

deltas.old: A back door with no handle on this side. Nothing about it is any of your business tonight.
deltas.new: The back door has no handle on this side. You have nothing to bring through it.

deltas.old: Two men at the far table, talking to each other. Nothing here for you tonight.
deltas.new: The two at the far table have their heads together and their voices under the room. Neither looks up when you stop beside them.

deltas.old: Pink lacquer, gone before you turned your head. The fronts on this stretch take a moment to remember they were busy, and not one of them looks north after it.
deltas.new: Pink lacquer and a black wheel-rim, already past the end of the colonnade by the time your head comes round. The calling starts again a beat later, one shopfront at a time down the row.

deltas.old: A modest hanging board, burgundy and brass, lettered COYLE AND SONS in a hand that cost more than the paint. The frontage behind it is one narrow door and a clean window. Everything that actually moves through this firm goes round the side, on wagons, after dark.
deltas.new: The hanging board is burgundy and brass, lettered COYLE AND SONS in a signwriter's hand. Under it the frontage is one narrow door and one clean window; the doors standing open on this building are all round the side, facing the alley.

deltas.old: A brass bell nobody rings, a blotter, and a small mirror angled so the man behind the counter can watch the door without appearing to.
deltas.new: Dust in the dome of the brass bell, a clean blotter under it, and a small mirror screwed to the shelf edge. Look into the mirror and you are looking at the doorway.

deltas.old: A desk set at an angle that lets the scribe see the street and the street see nothing. There is a second chair, and it has been sat in recently.
deltas.new: The desk stands at an angle to the window: the page faces the wall, the scribe faces the street. The second chair is drawn up close on the page side and pushed back at a slant.
